```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_survival <- requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_survival)
```

A package for statistical analysis must give the right numbers. Every estimator and model of
SurvX was checked in three ways:

1. **accuracy**: the results are compared with those of the established reference packages, on
   simulated and real data sets with and without ties, strata, delayed entry, clusters and
   weights;
2. **statistical properties**: a Monte Carlo study checks bias, standard errors and the coverage
   of confidence intervals, and the size and power of the tests;
3. **stability**: difficult data (few events, heavy censoring, ties, separation, extreme scales,
   collinearity) must give either a correct result, a fit flagged as not converged, or a clear
   error, never a silent wrong answer; and results must not depend on the order of the rows or the
   units of time.

The suite is in the directory `validation` of the source repository
(<https://github.com/stats9/SurvX>); `Rscript run_validation.R` runs it and writes one text file
and one PDF of figures. A run takes about 20 minutes in quick mode and several hours in full
mode.

## Agreement with the reference packages

Largest difference over all data sets of the full run (82 data sets, up to $n = 20000$):

| SurvX | Reference | Quantity | Largest difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `km()` | `survival::survfit` | survival, Greenwood SE, median and CI | $10^{-15}$ |
| `logrank_test()` | `survival::survdiff` | log-rank, Peto-Peto, stratified | relative $3 \times 10^{-6}$ |
| `rmst()` | `survival::survfit`, `survRM2::rmst2` | RMST and its SE | $10^{-11}$ |
| `hazard_np()` | `survival::survfit(ctype = 1)` | Nelson-Aalen | $10^{-15}$ |
| `aj()` | `cmprsk::cuminc`, `survival::survfit` | cumulative incidence | $10^{-14}$ |
| `gray_test()` | `cmprsk::cuminc` | Gray's statistics | $10^{-11}$ |
| `cox()` | `survival::coxph` | coefficients, variances, log-likelihood | $10^{-6}$ |
| `cox()` with `tt()` | `survival::coxph(tt = )` | coefficients, variances | $10^{-8}$ |
| `ph_test()` | `survival::cox.zph` | score tests (4 transforms) | $10^{-7}$ |
| `predict(cox)` | `survival::survfit.coxph` | predicted survival | $10^{-9}$ |
| `residuals(cox)` | `survival::residuals.coxph` | martingale, deviance, scaled Schoenfeld | $10^{-8}$ |
| `fg()` | `cmprsk::crr` | coefficients, robust variance, predictions | $10^{-7}$ |
| `fg()` with delayed entry | `survival::finegray` + `coxph` | coefficients, robust variance | $10^{-7}$ |
| `csc()` | `survival::coxph`, `riskRegression::CSC` | coefficients, variances, predicted CIF | $10^{-6}$ |
| `parsurv()` | `survival::survreg` | AFT coefficients, SEs, log-likelihood | $10^{-9}$ |
| `parsurv()` | `flexsurv::flexsurvreg`, `flexsurvspline` | log-likelihood, coefficients, SEs | optimiser tolerance |
| `cure()` | `flexsurvcure::flexsurvcure` | log-likelihood, predictions | optimiser tolerance |
| `brier_score()`, `auc_t()` | `riskRegression::Score` | Brier score, AUC | $10^{-14}$ |

"Optimiser tolerance" means that the reference package maximises the likelihood numerically
with its own stopping rule; where the results differ beyond it, SurvX reaches the higher
log-likelihood. `directcif()` has no other implementation in R; its likelihoods, scores and
information matrices were checked against independent code and numerical differentiation.

## A check you can run

The comparison with **survival** takes a few lines:

```{r}
library(SurvX)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1
ours <- cox(Event(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, lung)
ref <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = lung)
cbind(SurvX = coef(ours), survival = coef(ref), difference = coef(ours) - coef(ref))
max(abs(vcov(ours) - vcov(ref)))
```

## Statistical properties

In the Monte Carlo study (1000 replications for each of $n$ = 200, 500 and 1000), data were
generated from each model with known parameters. Across the models, the mean standard error
matched the empirical standard deviation of the estimates (ratios mostly between 0.95 and 1.05),
the 95% confidence intervals covered close to 95%, and the tests held their level (log-rank 4-6%,
Gray 4-5%, `ph_test()` 5-6% at the 5% level). Two findings shaped the package:

* with delayed entry, the robust variance of the Fine-Gray model, which treats the weights as
  known (as `survival::finegray` does), was 5-11% too small; `fg(..., variance = "bootstrap")` was
  added for this case;
* with the Kaplan-Meier transform and $n = 300$, the size of the proportional hazards test was
  above 5% in one design, identically for `survival::cox.zph` on the same data: a property of the
  test, not of the code.

## Speed

Median time of one fit with $n = 10000$ and 5 covariates (one core):

| Model | SurvX | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Cox | 0.01 s | `coxph` 0.03 s |
| Fine-Gray | 0.01 s | `crr` 154 s; `finegray` + `coxph` 11 s |
| cause-specific Cox | 0.01 s | `riskRegression::CSC` 0.07 s |
| Weibull PH | 0.02 s | `flexsurvreg` 0.17 s |
| generalized gamma | 0.36 s | `flexsurvreg` 2.8 s |
| Royston-Parmar spline | 0.03 s | `flexsurvspline` 1.6 s |
| mixture cure | 0.03 s | `flexsurvcure` 2.9 s |

The full tables, figures and session information of each run are written by the suite itself.
